newsitem.title: UK: Metals Outlook - LME to get back into its stride.
newsitem.headline: Metals Outlook - LME to get back into its stride.

text.p: Business is expected to pick up in non-ferrous metals this week, with the holiday period over and all participants back in the market, analysts said.
On the London Metal Exchange (LME) a solid performance in copper last week, given added spice by a warehouse stock decline on Friday, had put the market on course for more gains.
"People are just a bit more friendly towards the market at the moment. It's not unusual - you always see a bit of a run-up in January," one veteran trader said.
However, the real test this week would be whether copper, aluminium and the rest of the metals could sustain the advances notched up during the last holiday-truncated week.
"It was pitifully thin at times, so one has to be wary of it," the trader said.
Three months copper prices concluded last week at $2,193 a tonne, up from $2,127 the previous Friday. The cash/three months backwardation also widened last week to stand at $110.
"There is a general mood of optimism around for an early new year rally, which looks plausible if spreads continue to prevent major selling pressure," another trader said.
The other focus for the copper market was inventories and whether last Friday's 2,125-tonne decline heralded another sustained run of stock drawdowns.
LME copper stocks currently stand at 123,225 tonnes -- above the November 1996 6-1/4 year low of 90,050 tonnes, but still critically low.
"With the return to normal business after the December break demand should pick up," said William Adams, analyst at LME trader Rudolf Wolff and Co.
"A drawdown of metal is then likely to see both the backwardation and price rise, and with such low stock levels short-term price spikes are likely," he added.
Aluminium could struggle if prices were unable to clear the $1,570/75 level on the charts. Last week, the market closed at $2,154.
Analysts said that the market could be further inhibited by inventories, which rose on both occasions last week after an encouraging run of drawdowns.
Elsewhere on the LME, sub-zero temperatures in Europe would help lift replacement battery demand from the auto sector and consequently boost lead prices.
"I think we might have seen the lows in this market last year ($666)," one analyst said.
Also, the recently depressed nickel market should benefit if last week's halt in stock increases continued. Nickel closed at $6,605 a tonne on Friday.
